title: Double-Slit Diffraction
short_intro: Double-slit diffraction is the combined optical phenomenon of interference arising from two coherent sources and diffraction occurring due to the finite width of each individual slit. The resulting intensity distribution is a product of single-slit diffraction envelope and double-slit interference fringes.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of intensity distribution, conditions for missing orders, positions of principal maxima and minima, and comparison with pure double-slit interference.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous mathematical derivation of the resultant intensity pattern combining diffraction and interference factors, analytical determination of missing (absent) spectra, and angular width calculations.

prerequisites: Fraunhofer Diffraction at a Single Slit

concept_notes.heading: Superposition of Interference and Diffraction
bullets: In a double-slit arrangement where each slit has a finite width a and are separated by center-to-center distance d, both diffraction and interference occur simultaneously.
The overall intensity pattern is formed by modulating the rapid interference fringes by the slow-varying single-slit diffraction envelope.
The diffraction factor governs the overall amplitude envelope, while the interference factor determines the rapid oscillations within that envelope.

concept_notes.heading: Resultant Amplitude and Intensity
bullets: The amplitude due to a single slit of width a at an angle θ is given by A = A0(sin α/α), where α = (πa sin θ)/λ.
The resultant amplitude from two identical slits separated by distance d introduces a phase difference 2β, where β = (πd sin θ)/λ.
The resultant intensity is expressed as I = I<sub>0</sub> (sin α / α)<sup>2</sup> cos<sup>2</sup> β.

concept_notes.heading: Conditions for Maxima and Minima
bullets: Interference maxima occur when d sin θ = nλ, where n = 0, ±1, ±2, ...
Diffraction minima (zeroes of the envelope) occur when a sin θ = mλ, where m = ±1, ±2, ±3, ... (excluding m = 0 which corresponds to the central maximum).
The angular width of the central diffraction maximum is twice that of the single slit: 2θ = 2λ/a.

concept_notes.heading: Missing Orders in Double-Slit Diffraction
bullets: A missing order (or absent spectrum) occurs when an interference maximum coincides with a diffraction minimum.
The mathematical condition is given by d sin θ = nλ and a sin θ = mλ, which simplifies to d/a = n/m.
If the ratio d/a is an integer (e.g., d = 2a), then the 2nd, 4th, 6th... interference orders will be completely missing from the pattern.

derivations.title: Derivations of Intensity Distribution in Double-Slit Diffraction
derivations.conditions: Fraunhofer diffraction regime using two parallel rectangular slits of width a and center separation d illuminated by monochromatic light of wavelength λ normal to the screen.
steps: Consider two identical slits, each of width a, spanning from x = -a/2 to a/2 for the first slit, and x = d-a/2 to d+a/2 for the second slit.
Integrate the complex amplitude over the aperture of the first slit to obtain the single-slit amplitude component: E<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>0</sub> (sin α / α), where α = (πa sin θ)/λ.

Account for the path difference between corresponding points in the two slits, which gives a phase difference φ = 2β = 2(πd sin θ)/λ between the secondary wavelets originating from the centers of the two slits.
Sum the complex amplitudes from both slits using phasor addition or direct integration: E<sub>net</sub> = E<sub>1</sub> + E<sub>2</sub> = A<sub>0</sub> (sin α / α) [1 + e<sup>i 2β</sup>].
Multiply the net amplitude by its complex conjugate to find the resultant intensity: I = I<sub>0</sub> (sin α / α)<sup>2</sup> cos<sup>2</sup> β.

derivations.title: Derivation of Missing Orders Condition
derivations.conditions: Interference maxima coinciding with diffraction minima.
steps: Write the general condition for interference maxima: d sin \theta = n lambda, where n = 0, pm 1, pm 2, \dots
Write the general condition for diffraction minima: a sin \theta = m lambda, where m = pm 1, pm 2, pm 3, \dots
Equate the expression for sin \theta from both equations: \frac{n lambda}{d} = \frac{m lambda}{a}.
Simplify the relation to find the ratio of slit separation to slit width: \frac{d}{a} = \frac{n}{m}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity vs. Angle (or Position) Graph for Double-Slit Diffraction
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-shaped envelope curve representing (sin alpha / alpha)^2, enclosing rapid oscillatory interference fringes representing cos^2 \beta. Show zero intensity where the envelope touches the axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes how the single-slit diffraction envelope modulates the double-slit interference fringes, causing certain interference peaks to vanish.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in PGT/TGT to identify missing orders or sketch the combined diffraction-interference pattern.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Young's Double Slit vs. Double-Slit Diffraction Comparison
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two side-by-side graphs: one with uniform intensity peaks (ideal Young's slits where a -> 0) and one with envelope modulation (finite slit width a).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that ideal interference assumes point sources, whereas real optical slits exhibit diffraction attenuation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions distinguishing pure interference from combined interference-diffraction.

solved_numericals.question: In a double-slit diffraction pattern, the slit width is 0.1 mm and the separation between the centers of two slits is 0.5 mm. Find which order of interference maximum will be missing inside the central diffraction maximum.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: slit width a = 0.1 mm, separation d = 0.5 mm.
Use the missing order condition: d/a = n/m.
For the first missing order inside the central envelope, set m = 1, which gives n = 5.

solved_numericals.question: Light of wavelength 500 nm falls normally on a double slit. Each slit has a width of 0.2 mm and they are spaced 1.0 mm apart center-to-center. Calculate the total number of interference fringes contained within the central diffraction envelope.
solution_steps: Identify parameters: lambda = 500 \times 10^{-9} m, a = 0.2 \times 10^{-3} m, d = 1.0 \times 10^{-3} m.
The central diffraction envelope spans from the first diffraction minimum on the left (m = -1) to the first diffraction minimum on the right (m = 1).
The angle \theta for the first diffraction minimum is given by a sin \theta = lambda => sin \theta = lambda / a.
The interference maxima are given by d sin \theta = n lambda. Substitute sin \theta = lambda / a to find the interference order at the diffraction minimum: d (lambda / a) = n lambda => n = d / a.

This means the 5th interference maximum coincides with the 1st diffraction minimum. Therefore, the interference fringes from n = -4 to n = 4 lie entirely inside the central envelope, plus the central peak n = 0.
Total number of complete fringes in the central maximum = 2(5 - 1) + 1 = 9, or count orders n = 0, pm 1, pm 2, pm 3, pm 4 (total 9 fringes).

solved_numericals.question: An optical arrangement uses slits of width 0.05 mm separated by 0.25 mm. If monochromatic light of wavelength 589 nm is used, determine the ratio of the intensity of the first subsidiary interference maximum to the principal central maximum.
solution_steps: Write the intensity formula: I = I_0 (sin alpha / alpha)^2 cos^2 \beta.
For the central principal maximum, alpha = 0 and \beta = 0, so I = I_0.

For the first subsidiary interference maximum, determine its position using \beta approx pi / 2 (or solve d sin \theta = lambda / 2 for first interference peak away from center, though strictly n = 0, 1...). Wait, let's use \beta = pi/2 for the first interference maximum outside n=0 (i.e., n=1, \beta = pi d sin\theta / lambda = pi d (lambda / d)/lambda = pi). Correction: for n=1, \beta = pi. Let's compute alpha corresponding to n=1.
From d/a = 0.25 / 0.05 = 5, we have d = 5a. Thus alpha = pi a sin \theta / lambda = (pi a / lambda) (n lambda / d) = n pi (a/d) = n pi / 5.

For the first interference maximum (n = 1), alpha = pi / 5 radians (or 36 degrees), and \beta = pi radians (where cos^2 \beta = 1 if evaluated at peak, wait, cos^2( pi ) = 1, but for n=1, \beta = pi radians gives cos^2(pi) = 1).
Calculate the diffraction factor: (sin(pi/5) / (pi/5))^2. Since pi/5 rad = 36°, sin(36°) approx 0.5878, pi/5 approx 0.6283.
Multiply by cos^2 \beta (which is 1 at the interference maximum): I / I_0 approx 0.875.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes Fraunhofer conditions where both the source and the screen are effectively at infinity (achieved using lenses in laboratory setups).
Assumes incident light is perfectly monochromatic and coherent.
Neglects edge effects and finite thickness of the partition between the two slits.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Double-slit diffraction pattern is identical to Young's double-slit interference pattern.
common_misconceptions.correct: Young's double-slit pattern assumes infinitely narrow slits (constant intensity envelope), whereas real slits produce diffraction modulation that varies the fringe intensities and causes missing orders.
common_misconceptions.why: Finite slit width introduces single-slit diffraction envelope terms (sin alpha / alpha)^2 that modulate the interference fringes.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Missing orders mean light is absorbed at those positions.
common_misconceptions.correct: Light is redistributed, not destroyed; missing orders correspond to points where the interference condition yields a maximum but the diffraction envelope has a zero (minimum).
common_misconceptions.why: Destructive interference from individual slit components cancels the light amplitude precisely where an interference maximum is expected.

quick_revision: Total Intensity = Single-slit diffraction factor × Double-slit interference factor: I = I_0 (sin alpha / alpha)^2 cos^2 \beta.
Missing order condition: d / a = n / m.
Number of interference fringes in central maximum depends directly on the ratio 2d/a.
